Speaker: Shashikanth (≈30 s). Introduce the team and the topic: Transformers are the architecture behind BERT, GPT and almost every modern NLP system. Our question: what do they really give, and at what cost, when you only have a normal laptop and limited labelled data?

Speaker: Shashikanth (≈45 s). Before 2017 NLP models read sentences word by word. The Transformer by Vaswani et al. removed recurrence and kept only attention. That gave parallel training and made huge pre-training possible: BERT, GPT and others. Aim of the project: explain the architecture and measure its benefit experimentally.

Speaker: Shashikanth (≈60 s). Explain Q, K, V: each word asks a question (query), every word offers a key, the softmax of their dot products gives attention weights, and the output is a weighted mix of values. Several heads run in parallel. Layers are stacked with residual connections and layer normalisation. For classification we take the [CLS] vector and add a softmax layer.

Speaker: Shaeed (≈60 s). In one sentence: the papers tell us which model is accurate, but not what it costs or how many labels it needs. We searched Google Scholar and Web of Science (transformer OR BERT AND sentiment / text classification, plus Lithuanian). There are three model families; we use encoder-only models for classification. What the studies show: first, Transformers are the most accurate, above 90% on SST-2 against 79 to 83% for classical models. Second, without pre-training small data is a problem: in Lithuania naive Bayes at 0.735 beat LSTM and CNN at 0.706. Third, Lithuanian now has pre-trained models, LitLat BERT and BERT/T5, and open Llama2 models. What is missing, our gap: these studies report accuracy, but a student with a laptop also needs to know the cost, how many labels are needed, and whether a ready-made model is enough. We measure all three on one laptop CPU.

Speaker: Shaeed (≈45 s). Dataset: Stanford Sentiment Treebank, binary. The official validation set is our test set, 2,000 training sentences are the dev set. Ten models in four groups. Everything runs on the same laptop CPU so times are comparable.

Speaker: Shashikanth (≈40 s). The program is a pipeline of nine scripts. The key one is the fine-tuning script: give it any model name from the Hugging Face hub and a number of training examples. All results are stored with predictions, so the report script computes tables, figures and statistical tests.

Speaker: Shashikanth (≈60 s). Ranking of all ten models. Classical TF-IDF models reach 81.9–82.9%, the BiLSTM 82.8%, our fine-tuned Transformers up to 88.8% with only 8,000 labelled sentences. The ready-made DistilBERT-SST2 reaches 91.1%. Zero-shot, with no labels at all, still gets 81.8%.

Speaker: Shashikanth (≈45 s). The gain is not free: a TF-IDF model trains in seconds and classifies in microseconds; Transformers need minutes to tens of minutes of CPU training and milliseconds per sentence. For most applications that is still perfectly acceptable.

Speaker: Shaeed (≈50 s). Same random subsets for both models. With very few labels TF-IDF cannot learn the vocabulary, while BERT-small already knows English from pre-training. This confirms the Lithuanian finding that pre-training, not the neural network as such, is what makes the difference on small data.

Speaker: Shaeed (≈45 s). Bag-of-words models lose most on sentences with negation and contrast, because 'not good' contains the word 'good'. Transformers keep their accuracy much better. The heat-map shows how attention links the words in such a sentence – but, as Jain and Wallace warn, attention is an illustration, not a proof of reasoning.

Speaker: Shaeed (≈60 s). Summarise the answers to the research questions and give the practical recommendation: first try a public in-domain model, otherwise fine-tune a compact Transformer on a few thousand labels; use TF-IDF only when latency or hardware are extremely limited. Future work: Lithuanian data with LitLat BERT. Invite questions.
